title: Bayesline founders say AI is causing them to lead differently
excerpt: The founders of fintech startup Bayesline said AI's pace is changing their approach to feedback and healthy disagreements.
content_html:
These fintech founders say AI makes fast and candid feedback more important

By Tim Paradis

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-22T10:41:01.262Z

Years before they started a company together, Sebastian Janisch and Misha van Beek became accidental roommates under tough circumstances.

Van Beek had expected to crash at Janisch's New York apartment for a couple of weeks. Then the COVID-19 pandemic hit. The arrangement evolved into two-week rotations between the apartment's sole bedroom and its couch, while they each worked from the small kitchen island.

Living in close quarters exposed their differences: Janisch, the orderly future CEO, and van Beek, who jokingly describes himself as "complete chaos." It also taught them, they said, that cofounders don't need matching work styles as much as they need sufficient trust to make decisions quickly — especially as AI accelerates the pace of software development.

Janisch and van Beek are trying to turn that insight into a workplace culture at Bayesline, a New York fintech, which recently closed a $4 million funding round after earlier backing from Y Combinator. They said they encourage their small staff of about half a dozen to challenge others' ideas, regardless of title or tenure, so the team can move fast.

Their mantra, Janisch said, is "hard on content, soft on people."

Welcoming disagreement

Bayesline makes portfolio-analytics software that helps investment managers understand risk and evaluate performance. The expectation of giving candid feedback to quickly solve problems applies to everyone — from the company's first employee to a recently hired software engineer in his 20s, Janisch said. He said he wants that engineer to feel comfortable saying, "Sebastian, I've reviewed your code. It makes no sense. Why did you do it?"

That is part of how the company improves, Janisch said. He said that giving that kind of feedback to a CEO is something he "100% would not have done" early in his career in his native Germany. The founders say they want workers to feel no hesitation about pointing out problems so they can be solved sooner.

Janisch and van Beek had to learn to manage their differences during the six months they were roommates. Janisch would turn the shirts van Beek had hung up to dry so they faced the same direction.

Their occasional disagreements are more substantive now. To hash out an issue, they might spend 20 minutes talking it through before reaching a consensus, Janisch said. If they hit an impasse, the founder with deeper expertise makes the decision while the other steps aside, he said. It's a way to keep things moving.

"A decision is better than no decision," Janisch said, adding that you can correct it afterward if it's wrong and, often, it's not.

Moving fast without losing judgment

The need to quickly make a call — and, at times, to disagree and commit — has only grown as AI lets a small team produce more code, Janisch said. That higher output means there is more work to review.

That is why Bayesline wants staffers who are fluent in using AI yet also have enough experience in finance or software engineering to know when the technology has gone astray.

"We hire people that are good with AI, but their experience is still in the old world, so they can judge whether the AI is doing a good job," van Beek said.

The founders' desire for decisive action doesn't mean they automatically see tenure as the best measure of judgment. The young engineer has what the founders see as unusually useful knowledge of how portfolio managers think about analytics. Another engineering hire, with a dozen years' experience at a financial institution, gives the startup a steady presence when it meets with enterprise clients, Janisch said.

That approach continues to shape how Bayesline operates. Recently, the young engineer suggested new tools to help the team handle the growing volume of code to review. After looking into the proposal, the founders adopted it.

Janisch said their response was simple: "That's exactly how we should change it."
